newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala labor lukewarm on U.S. sweatshop code.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala labor lukewarm on U.S. sweatshop code.

text.p: GUATEMALA CITY, April 14 - Guatemalan unions who have complained of widespread abuses of workers rights in clothing factories, said on Monday a U.S. code of conduct designed to combat sweatshop labor was not tough enough.

U.S President Bill Clinton on Monday threw his support behind the code, under which companies would agree to have independent auditors monitor compliance with rules such as minimum wage, no child labor and a maximum 60-hour work week.

But union leaders in Guatemala, which has been under scrutiny by the United States for suspected violations of worker rights in textile assembly plants, feared the auditors would give their seal of approval too easily and not stand up for workers.

"This policy would cheat the working class. Independent monitoring would work only if it were in consultation with workers, unionized and otherwise," said Julio Coj, of the Guatemalan Workers Labor Union.
Coj and other labor leaders said non-governmental organizations such as religious, human rights and labor groups should be part of the monitoring process.

The code of conduct was the product of Clinton's "No Sweat" task force made up of U.S. clothing makers such as Nike Inc, L.L. Bean, and Liz Claiborne Inc., labor unions and human rights groups which banded together to recommend steps to ensure products were not made under exploitative conditions.

Companies that agree to the code would hire an auditor, such as the international firm Ernst & Young, for regular monitoring. Manufacturers in compliance could use a "No Sweat" label on clothes to guarantee they were not made under sweatshop conditions.
Coj said the code was likely to be widely ignored and that most companies buying products made in Guatemala would not investigate whether the business was complying with the code.
Stephen Coats of the U.S./Guatemala Labor Education Project said Clinton's endorsement should help pressure U.S. retailers to buy from "No Sweat" factories.
But the code needs some major fine-tuning, said Coats. For example, complying with the minimum wage is meaningless in Guatemala where that wage is not enough to live on.
Guatemalan business representatives were no more enthusiastic about the code than labor groups.

Guatemala does not need the U.S. code of conduct because businesses here developed their own code and independent auditing system, which three textile factories have accepted, said Luisa Fernandez, of the Guatemalan Exporters Guild.
